title: MSI Wrapper
html:
MSI Wrapper

MSI Wrapper can package an executable or script as a Windows Installer (.msi) file. Download and start the free edition, then select the executable to package.[3] To run a sequence of commands, select a .bat file as the input rather than packaging cmd.exe.[1]

Configure the execution context and other installer properties carefully:

These values can be changed when packaging a custom binary.

Continue through the remaining wizard pages and select Build to generate the installer.[1]

Verify the wrapped command's execution context

For a test package, wrap a .bat file that records its token instead of assuming the MSI's elevation setting applies to its child process.[4] In the wizard, choose the System security context rather than User and choose a per-machine, elevated installation when that is the intended path.[5] The System option does not bypass authorization: a non-admin still needs an elevated installation route, such as the two-policy AlwaysInstallElevated misconfiguration or a privileged installer workflow.[2] Choosing User instead runs the wrapped command with the installing user's context, which may be necessary for user-specific or network resources.[5]

@echo off
whoami /all > "C:\Users\Public\msi-wrapper-context.txt"
exit /b 0

Build the MSI with this batch file as input, then run it on the test host and inspect the recorded identity and privileges.[4] MSI Wrapper maps a nonzero batch exit code to installation error 1603, so the explicit zero exit avoids a false failure after a successful test.[4] The output file is a test artifact; do not infer SYSTEM execution merely from a successful msiexec exit or a quiet install.[5][6]

msiexec.exe /i "C:\Users\Public\context-test.msi" /qn /norestart /L*V "C:\Users\Public\context-test.log"
type "C:\Users\Public\msi-wrapper-context.txt"

/qn silences the MSI UI, not necessarily the wrapped executable's own UI.[6][7] For a wrapped installer, set its supported silent arguments in the wizard; MSI Wrapper's dynamic WRAPPED_ARGUMENTS property is a PRO feature.[1][7] See the WiX custom-action approach if you need direct control over custom-action sequencing and impersonation.

Warning

Creating an MSI does not by itself grant elevated privileges. Whether installation is elevated depends on Windows Installer policy, package context, and user authorization. Microsoft warns that enabling AlwaysInstallElevated for both the user and computer lets non-administrators install packages with system privileges.[2]
